items.question: How does fire abide equally in all trees?
premises: Fire is the same in every tree
Its presence is not divided by different trees
The analogy illustrates equal abiding
items.inference: Just as fire abides equally in all trees, the supreme reality abides equally everywhere.
items.plain_english: O beautiful one, just as the same fire stands equally in every tree, so it abides.

items.question: How does brahman become manifest through churning wood and the like?
premises: Fire becomes manifest by churning wood
What was latent becomes visible through a process
Brahman is spoken of as manifest in a similar way
items.inference: Brahman, though present, is said to become manifest through an appropriate means, like fire from wood.
uncertainties: rucyate may mean 'is pleasing' or 'is called'; taken here as 'is called/spoken of'
items.plain_english: O goddess, through the churning of wood and the like, brahman is said to become manifest.

items.question: What becomes possible beyond through abandoning both dharma and adharma?
premises: Dharma and adharma are paired opposites
Abandonment of both transcends their duality
The whole can be considered in relation to the beyond
items.inference: By abandoning both dharma and adharma, one moves toward what lies beyond them.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: And also, by abandoning both dharma and adharma, all is directed beyond.

items.question: What is the true cause of impurity notions about urine and the like?
premises: One should reflect on one's own urine and similar substances
Impurity is attributed to them by convention
Delusion alone is identified as the cause
items.inference: The sense of impurity regarding urine and the like arises from delusion, not from their intrinsic nature.
items.plain_english: One should consider that, regarding one's own urine and the like, delusion alone is the cause.

items.question: By what can feces, the abode of various beings, be truly polluted?
premises: Feces serves as an abode for various beings
It is commonly regarded as impure
The question challenges who or what truly pollutes it
items.inference: If feces already supports many forms of life, its supposed pollution cannot be established as intrinsic.
items.plain_english: That feces is the abode of various beings; by whom, then, is it polluted?

items.question: What is prescribed in expiations for release from brahmin-killing and the like?
premises: Expiations are prescribed in scripture
Brahmin-killing and similar acts require release
Such prescriptions are conventionally stated
items.inference: Scriptural expiations address grave acts like brahmin-killing within a conventional framework.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: In expiations, it is stated for liberation from brahmin-killing and the like.

items.question: How does a woman's menses relate to the birth of the body?
premises: A woman's menses is part of bodily generation
The body is born from such material causes
What is deemed impure is also generative
items.inference: Since the body is born from menstrual substance, its condemnation as impure is problematic.
items.plain_english: O supreme goddess, from a woman's menses the body itself is born.

items.question: What is identified as the generative seed of a man?
premises: Male contribution to generation is named
The seed is called the seminal drop
This parallels the female generative substance
items.inference: The man's seed is called the seminal drop, a bodily substance involved in birth.
items.plain_english: And the seed of a man is called the seminal drop.

items.question: Why is there no pollution in scripture and the like from the standpoint of śiva's nature?
premises: From the nature of śiva all is grounded in that reality
Scripture and similar things are considered within that view
Pollution is denied in that state
items.inference: When seen through the nature of śiva, there is truly no pollution in scripture and the like.
uncertainties: śāstha may be a variant spelling of śāstra
items.plain_english: Then, by the nature of śiva, there is indeed no pollution in scripture and the like.

items.question: How does the path of knowledge reveal all for the undifferentiated one?
premises: The path of knowledge is invoked
The undifferentiated state transcends divisions
All is encompassed in that realization
items.inference: Through the path of knowledge, all is understood in the undifferentiated reality.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: O beautiful one, by the path of knowledge, all belongs to the undifferentiated.

items.question: What is the relationship between the seed in the mother's womb and the child?
premises: The seed in the mother's womb is the origin of the child
The child arises from that seed
There is no doubt about this identity of origin
items.inference: The seed in the mother's womb is indeed the child; there is no doubt.
items.plain_english: The seed in the mother's womb is indeed the child; there is no doubt.

items.question: If that is considered polluted, how can anything else be regarded as auspicious?
premises: The generative seed is sometimes deemed polluted
The child and body arise from that same source
If the source is polluted, other things would still be auspicious by contrast
items.inference: Calling the generative source polluted while deeming other things auspicious is inconsistent.
uncertainties: The logical force is rhetorical and somewhat compressed
items.plain_english: If that is joined with pollution, then everything else would be auspicious.

items.question: What does the speaker declare after knowing this truth?
premises: The speaker claims knowledge of the matter
The goddess is addressed directly
A declaration follows from that knowledge
items.inference: Having known this, the speaker proceeds to declare the truth to the goddess.
items.plain_english: Having known that, O supreme goddess, O fair-faced one, I tell you.

items.question: Why are conventional class identities like vaiśya and śūdra ultimately denied?
premises: Social classes are conventionally distinguished
The verse negates these identities as ultimate
The address to the goddess frames a higher teaching
items.inference: From the higher standpoint, a vaiśya is not truly a vaiśya and a śūdra is not truly a śūdra.
items.plain_english: O supreme goddess, a vaiśya is not a vaiśya, and a śūdra is not a śūdra.

items.question: What should be known with certainty as the reality of all beings?
premises: Conventional distinctions have been negated
A single reality underlies all
This is to be known with certainty
items.inference: One should know with certainty that the supreme self is the reality of all.
items.plain_english: Know with certainty that the supreme self belongs to all.

items.question: How is everything in the middle of a village regarded as polluted by feces and urine?
premises: Village spaces contain waste substances
Feces, urine, and the like are considered polluting
Everything there is described as tainted
items.inference: By conventional standards, all within the village may be seen as polluted by waste.
uncertainties: ṣūditam is an unusual form; taken as 'polluted/tainted'
items.plain_english: Everything in the middle of the village is polluted by feces, urine, and the like.

items.question: What happens to all that pollution when it merges into the Gaṅgā?
premises: Polluted substances may flow into the Gaṅgā
The Gaṅgā is regarded as purifying
Merging changes the status of what was polluted
items.inference: When all merges into the Gaṅgā, its polluted status is no longer held in the same way.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: O goddess, when all of that has merged into the Gaṅgā.

items.question: What is the real cause of the faults attributed to impurity and urine?
premises: Faults are attributed to impurity and urine
Such attributions depend on perception and convention
Delusion alone is named as the cause
items.inference: The faults seen in impurity and urine are caused by delusion alone.
items.plain_english: Whatever faults are seen in impurity and urine, delusion alone is the cause.

items.question: How can the supreme state be attained through substances like blood?
premises: Blood and similar substances are conventionally impure
The verse asserts attainment of the supreme state through them
This challenges ordinary purity distinctions
items.inference: Even through substances like blood, the supreme state can be attained.
uncertainties: The ritual or doctrinal context of 'pradhānena' is not fully explicit
items.plain_english: By means of blood and the like, the supreme state is attained.

items.question: Why should the body, whose cause is semen, be censured by anyone?
premises: Semen is identified as a cause of all bodies
The body arises from that generative substance
Censuring the body contradicts its causal origin
items.inference: If semen is the cause of the body, there is no basis for censuring that body.
uncertainties: The compound 'deha' is taken as referring to the body in context
items.plain_english: Semen is the cause of all; by whom, then, is that body censured?

items.question: Who would not be a violator of the teacher's bed at the time of birth?
premises: Birth involves passage through the mother's womb
Violating the teacher's bed is a grave transgression in convention
The verse uses this as a reductio argument
items.inference: If conventional impurity logic were applied strictly, everyone would be guilty at birth, showing the absurdity of such judgments.
uncertainties: The rhetorical force depends on traditional associations of guru-talpa-ga
items.plain_english: When, at the time of birth, who would not be one who violates the teacher's bed?

items.question: Who is declared to be the one mother of countless universes?
premises: Countless universes are mentioned
A single mother of them is affirmed
The speaker identifies herself as that reality
items.inference: The speaker declares herself to be the one essential mother of countless universes.
items.plain_english: I alone, in my own form, am the one mother of countless universes.

items.question: How does the analogy of pot-space illustrate apparent division within space?
premises: A pot creates an apparent division in space
The space inside the pot is called pot-space
This division is due to the limiting adjunct, not to space itself
items.inference: Just as pot-space appears divided by the pot, reality may appear divided by limiting conditions.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically incomplete and continues into the next verse
items.plain_english: Just as, by the division of the potter's wheel, pot-space appears in the pot.

items.question: How should one understand apparent difference in space caused by the pot?
premises: In the pot, space appears as different
This difference is conditioned by the pot
One should reflect on this apparent division in space
items.inference: One should understand that difference in space is only apparent, conditioned by the pot.
uncertainties: The final compound member 'bhinna' is taken as qualifying the perceived difference
items.plain_english: In the pot it appears as different; one should consider that difference in space.
